source.title: Neural networks are more modular than single neurons suggest
source.authors: Shreya Saha; Benjamin K. Bergen; Meenakshi Khosla

record.tranche_reason: The study directly evaluates whether unit-level activity supports separate computations and reports cases where it does not, while showing functional separation at subspace level in its own experiments.
record.gate_note: The paper tests unit-level modularity using task-variance measures and causal ablation in RNNs. Its vision and language retrieval results assess subspace selectivity, not neuron-pole job explanations, so they are not recorded as rows for the claim versions. Results cited from prior work are not included.
record.test_reason: The study measures task-level functional modularity: whether two computations can be separated by ablating unit sets or learned subspaces. It does this in 256-unit cognitive-task RNNs, and with retrieval selectivity in vision and language models. It never explains neurons or neuron poles or estimates the share of neurons with one main job. It does not examine InceptionV1 neurons, build attribution graphs, or score explanations by simulated activations. The RNN unit-level results come from a different kind of system (small CTRNNs trained on cognitive tasks, not language models). They measure a different construct: task-variance specialization and double dissociation, not interpretable single-neuron jobs. The paper discusses mixed selectivity and superposition only as background. It neither tests nor uses the claim, so no version gets a verdict.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is broadly correct but too narrow. The authors conclude that lack of unit-level modularity often coexists with clear subspace-level functional modularity across all three domains: RNNs, vision models (content vs style) and language models (syntax vs semantics). Unit-level or permutation decompositions fail where invertible linear ones succeed. In RNNs, softplus networks are modular at every level including units, while tanh networks need orthogonal or linear maps. The learned subspaces also align differentially with visual and language cortex.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses task-variance measurements, learned linear decompositions, retrieval evaluation, and causal ablation; it does not use the cited neuron-pole explanation-and-validation procedure.
record.method_sensitivity: The outcome depends on activation function and decomposition level; in the Mante task, linear DDI increases with subspace dimension and plateaus around d ≈ 15–20.

fits_no_version.finding: Unit-level (permutation) decompositions show no or weak task modularity in tanh RNNs: Yang Anti vs DM1 unit DDI 0.00, Sinkhorn 0.08; Mante unit and orthogonal DDI near zero. Orthogonal or linear subspace decompositions do recover double dissociations: Yang tanh 0.37/0.47; Mante linear 0.277±0.026. Softplus RNNs are modular already at the unit level (74% specialized, DDI 0.59).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Networks lacking unit-level task modularity can still have causally separable task subspaces, and whether units are specialized depends on the activation function.

fits_no_version.finding: In pretrained vision models, permutation (unit-level) decompositions give near-chance content/style selectivity (Swin-B Rs≈1.10, Rc≈1.02), while invertible maps reach Rs=16.1, Rc=5.3 (Table 1, Table E11). In Pythia and GPT-2 XL, permutation gives weak syntax/semantics separation (GPT-2 XL Top-1 S1=0.00), while invertible maps reach high separation (Table E12). No rows record these results.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In vision and language models, neurons are not split by content versus style or syntax versus semantics, yet linear subspaces separate these functions.

record.problems: The directly relevant unit-level evidence concerns a small set of task pairs and RNN settings, not neuron-pole explanations or Qwen3. The paper does not report uncertainty for the central Yang FTV and DDI values. The checklist says the submission does not yet include a public code release and plans release for the camera-ready version, despite the paper’s stated code URL.
record.rows_left_out: No results directly bearing on the listed versions were omitted. Vision and language retrieval results, brain-alignment analyses, and the TDR baseline do not measure neuron-pole job shares or the other listed version outcomes.

untested.parts: No study of Qwen3-32B, neuron poles, explanations, or the ~90%/7%/2–4% shares.
No neuron-pole job shares in any language model, dense or MoE, at any scale. The LM results (Pythia 160M/410M, GPT-2 XL) concern syntax/semantics subspace retrieval.
No re-examination of InceptionV1 cat/car or other canonical polysemantic neurons, and no test of recursive generalization versus superposition.
No estimate of interpretable-neuron shares, or of how they change with tools, architecture or regularization.
No attribution graphs built from a model's own neurons, and no replacement-model reconstruction error.
No test of neuron explanations against where the neuron fires.
No simulation-based scoring of neuron explanations.

record.verdict_notes: The reader linked the RNN unit-level rows to V1 and labeled them limits_scope and challenges. Those links and labels are removed. V1 concerns interpretable single-neuron jobs in Qwen3-32B; these rows measure task-specialization modularity in small cognitive-task RNNs. Different construct, different system. The paper does not cite either original source. A code URL is given in the paper, but the checklist says code is not yet released.

versions.untested_parts: Does not study Qwen3-32B, explain positive or negative neuron poles, test explanations on held-out activations, or estimate the claimed 90%, 7%, and 2–4% shares. Its unit-level results concern task specialization in RNNs.
No estimates of the claimed neuron-pole shares across model scales, dense/MoE architectures, or models approaching trillions of parameters.
Does not re-examine InceptionV1 cat-and-car neurons or test recursive generalization against superposition.
Does not estimate interpretable-neuron shares in InceptionV1-sized models or test how those shares change with tools, architecture, or regularization.
Does not test attribution graphs built from a large model’s own neurons or compare their reconstruction error with a trained replacement model.
Does not test neuron explanations against held-out activating examples or measure their ability to predict firing.
Does not evaluate automated neuron-explanation scores by simulating activations on new text.

relation.reason: It argues unit-level selectivity misses subspace-level modularity, a related but different construct; it does not test any version.

tranche.reason: Measures task-level functional modularity (ablation DDI in 256-unit RNNs, retrieval selectivity in vision and language models), not whether neuron poles have one interpretable job, explanation validity or neuron circuits; bears on none of V1-V7. The reader's T5 is not supported.

source_check.notes: The study measures task modularity: unit vs subspace double dissociations, with FTV as the unit-specialization proxy. It does not measure neuron interpretability, so it bears on no version. Six versions-none rows carried observed or absent states. Set them to cannot_determine, as the record does for its other none rows. Table 1 is Swin Base.

statements.correction: Yang tanh Anti vs DM1: unit DDI 0.00, Sinkhorn 0.08, orthogonal 0.37, linear 0.47. Mante tanh RNN: unit and orthogonal DDI near zero at all d in {2,5,10,15,20,50}; only linear recovers a dissociation (DDI 0.277 ± 0.026 at d=15, mean ± s.d. across seeds). Swin-B permutation Rs 1.10, Rc 1.02; invertible Rs 16.1, Rc 5.3 (Table 1).
statements.problem: All numbers match: Yang tanh unit 0.00, Sinkhorn 0.08; Mante near zero; Swin-B Table 1 1.10/1.02 vs 16.1/5.3. But it files Mante's near-zero orthogonal DDI under unit-level (permutation) failures. It then says orthogonal or linear decompositions recover dissociations. In Mante, orthogonal fails and only linear succeeds. Also, the text is not truncated: the values are given.
